title: How to Stay on Top of Your Bills

body_markdown:
Keeping up with your expenses is becoming harder than ever, especially given how furiously energy costs have surged.[Gas, for instance, increased 33%](https://www.macrotrends.net/4453/us-gasoline-prices#google_vignette) from $3.48 to $4.63 per gallon since September 2025.


Unfortunately, the pain doesn’t end at the gas pump. Higher fuel costs are causing everything to rise from groceries and utilities to even fun activities like flying to your favorite vacation destination.


Sadly, there’s no magic solution to bring your expenses down or make them go away. However, with a little bit of organization, consistent habits, and a plan for unexpected expenses, you can make managing your money less stressful.


Whether you want to avoid late fees, pay down debt, or build your savings, these six strategies can help you take control of your monthly expenses and work toward greater financial stability.


## 1) Make a List of Your Expenses


It’s nearly impossible to get in front of bills without first understanding what they are, how much you owe, and when they’re due. Without the full picture, you won’t be able to create a realistic budget or determine how much money you have available for savings and other financial goals.


Therefore, get to know your enemy! Start by making a list of your regular monthly expenses. Include anything you can think of such as:


- Rent or mortgage payments
- Auto loan payments
- Utilities
- Insurance premiums
- Student loans
- Credit card balances (and minimums).


Don’t forget to also include those smaller, sneaky recurring expenses like streaming services, gym memberships, and app subscriptions. Connecting your financial accounts to a budgeting app like[Buxfer](https://www.buxfer.com/) can make it easier to find and detect them.


Next, separate your fixed expenses from variable expenses. Fixed expenses generally remain the same each month, while variable expenses, such as groceries, gasoline, and electricity, can fluctuate. For these, try to come up with a reasonable amount to budget such as the average of your last three payments or what you paid this time last year.


Finally, record each bill’s amount and due date in a spreadsheet, budgeting app, or calendar. Commit to a time each week to review this list and ensure that each item is getting paid one by one.


## 2) Setup As Many Bills for Autopay as Possible


With most expenses, there’s no reason to gamble missing a payment because you forgot to mail a check. Nearly all major companies now allow you to schedule recurring payments. This is great because it helps reduce the risk of forgetting a payment or incurring a late fee.


Begin by putting predictable expenses, such as loan payments, insurance premiums, and internet services on autopay. Depending on the provider, you may be able to choose to pay them on their due date or a few days earlier.


While using a credit card may be a convenient and easy way to earn points, be mindful that some companies now charge a processing fee. In these cases, it may be cheaper to have the payment drafted from your bank account rather than paid with a credit card.


## 3) Build Up Your Cash Buffer


Being aware of your bills and having them automatically paid is great and all, but what if the source of your stress is whether or not those payments will go through? This can be particularly challenging if you’ve gotten into the undesirable habit of living paycheck to paycheck.


To give you peace of mind and better flexibility, you need a cash buffer. A cash buffer is a sizeable amount of money you keep in your checking account to ensure it never goes to zero. For most households, this should be a minimum of approximately one to two times your average monthly expenses. For example, if you normally spend amount $5,000 in any given month, aim to have about $10,000 in your checking account.


The purpose of this money is help ensure that no bill or automatic payment is ever skipped or triggers an overdraft fee. It can also be used to help temporarily cover those unexpected, larger expenses that sometimes creep in like a medical bill. This will let you avoid relying on a credit card where you’ll eventually get hit with interest charges.


As one of your financial goals, make creating this buffer a priority. Each week, review your expenses to ensure more is coming in than going out. Let the excess money build in your checking account until you’ve got an amount that makes you feel comfortable.


## 4) Work on Your Emergency Fund


Beyond building a cash buffer, the next layer of financial protection to create is an[emergency fund](https://blog.buxfer.com/2022/05/16/how-to-build-up-an-emergency-fund/) . This is another reserve of cash that can help you cover larger, unplanned, and urgent expenses such as vehicle trouble, home repairs, appliance replacements, or even unemployment.


The goal of your emergency fund is to ensure that you don’t get into debt over this unwelcomed expense. Oftentimes, many people turn to high-interest credit cards or predatory loans looking for a way out. Some might even go so far as to borrow or liquidate their retirement savings. None of these are great alternatives!


Most financial professionals recommend that your emergency fund should be at least three to six months’ worth of essential living expenses. Similar to your cash buffer, start small by setting aside a certain amount each month. Then as debts get paid or your earnings increase, gradually increase your contributions.


It’s important to keep your emergency money somewhere safe and easily accessible, such as a reputable high-yield savings account. Don’t keep it in your checking account with your cash buffer because you might then be tempted to spend it.


## 5) Eliminate Debt One by One


Debt payments can really restrict your cash flow, leaving less money to stay on top of your bills. Credit card balances, auto loans, student loans, and even your mortgage can be particularly challenging – especially for those arrangements where the interest continues to grow against you.


That’s why it’s crucial to have a plan for paying down your debts. The less you owe, the less interest you’ll be charged, and the more money you’ll have available for your other financial priorities.


Start by making a list of all your debts: the outstanding balance, interest rate, minimum payment, and due date.


Next, choose a repayment strategy. Two popular options are the[debt snowball method](https://blog.buxfer.com/2021/12/27/how-does-the-debt-snowball-work/) and debt avalanche method:


- **The debt snowball method** focuses on the smallest outstanding balance first. After paying off that debt, you redirect the money toward the next-smallest balance. This approach can provide quick wins and help you stay motivated.
- **The debt avalanche method** prioritizes the debt with the highest interest rate. You make minimum payments on all other accounts and direct extra money toward the most expensive debt. Once it is paid off, you move to the next-highest interest rate. This approach can help minimize total interest costs.


Both methods are effective and praised by many. However, you should choose the one that makes you feel the most motivated.


Be cautious when considering debt consolidation or balance transfers. Although these options may advertise to simplify payments or reduce interest, fees, promotional terms, and repayment periods can affect the total cost. If you’re ever truly underwater, a reputable nonprofit credit counseling organization may also be a good resource to help evaluate your situation.


## 6) Challenge Your Expenses


Debt isn’t the only thing restricting your cash flow and keeping you from paying your bills. Even small changes across several spending categories can add up over time. Therefore, it’s critical to regularly review your purchases and make cuts where you can.


Start by looking through your credit and debit card purchases. What have you bought this month that you didn’t really need? It might be a streaming service that you don’t watch or a gym membership that you’re not exactly using.


Don’t stop there. Consider expenses you might think are fixed like auto insurance. If it’s been more than two years, chances are you could get a quote from another insurance provider that’s cheaper than what you’re paying now. Use that as leverage to negotiate a lower rate, or consider making the switch.


Repeat this strategy with as many of your other expenses as possible. By just taking a few minutes every month to focus on handful, you may free up hundreds or even thousands from your budget.


## The Bottom Line


Staying on top of your bills begins with understanding your expenses, organizing payment dates, and establishing reliable routines. Use autopay where appropriate, build a cash buffer to manage short-term gaps, and work toward an emergency fund that can protect you from unexpected expenses. These habits can reduce financial stress and make your monthly obligations more manageable.


At the same time, develop a realistic plan to eliminate debt and regularly review your expenses for potential savings. You do not have to make every change at once. Start with one or two manageable steps, review your progress each month, and adjust as needed. With consistency and planning, you can keep your bills under control and build a stronger financial future.
